strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem (RGBA/transparent text-to-video generation) and positions itself well relative to prior work (LayerDiffuse, AlphaVAE, Alfie, TransPixeler).

The design is simple and efficient: by embedding alpha into the existing Wan latent space with a feature-merge block plus LoRA/DoRA adapters, the method adds no extra inference cost, in contrast to TransPixeler which doubles the backbone. The 4-step, CFG-free inference via LightX2V is attractive for deployment.

The reported qualitative results (Figures 1, 10-18) are impressive, showing convincing semi-transparent objects, glow effects, and fine alpha details such as hair, which are known failure cases of prior methods.
The data pipeline is described in reasonable detail (13 matting sources, augmentation, manual caption verification), and the authors promise to release the model, which would benefit the community.
The paper is honest about limitations (missing alpha regions, unintended background debris in Figures 19-20).
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative metrics (e.g., alpha SAD/MAD, edge quality, FVD/CLIP-based measures) and no user study, despite the central claim of 'superior performance in visual quality, motion realism, and transparency rendering.' For a CVPR submission, the absence of any quantitative or human evaluation is a material weakness.

Comparison is limited to a single baseline (TransPixeler), and the comparison protocol appears biased: Wan-Alpha is prompted with detailed, style-tagged captions, while TransPixeler receives short prompts; resolutions, frame counts, and FPS also differ across systems, making the '15 times faster' speed claim and quality comparisons hard to interpret fairly.

The technical novelty is modest: the approach directly follows the LayerDiffuse strategy (latent transparency via VAE adaptation) adapted to the Wan video model, with LoRA/DoRA fine-tuning. No ablation studies are provided to justify design choices such as the composite losses (Eqs. 7-13), the hard/soft rendering scheme, the random background colors, or DoRA vs. LoRA for the DiT.

The text-to-video training set is extremely small (437 samples, of which 116 are 'videos with special effects from the Internet' with unclear provenance/licensing), and captions were manually refined for every sample. This raises both scalability concerns and reproducibility issues, since the dataset does not appear to be released.

The VAE lacks a KL penalty and 'directly predicts the latent Z'; the paper asserts this avoids latent-space over-high variance but offers no analysis or evidence (e.g., latent statistics, training stability comparisons) supporting this deviation from standard practice.

Several claims are unsupported or incomplete: the release URL in the abstract is blank; Figures 19-20 are cited as illustrating limitations but the surrounding narrative is thin; the claim that 'DoRA yields better semantic alignment and higher-quality video' is stated without any supporting experiment.

Only static-image frames are shown; motion realism and temporal consistency of the alpha channel across 81 frames cannot be verified from the manuscript, and no failure-case statistics are given to gauge how often the limitations in Section 3.4 occur.

strengths: Addresses a practically useful and underexplored problem: RGBA text-to-video generation, which has clear value for video editing, gaming, and sticker/emoji production.

The design is efficient and deployment-friendly: alpha information is injected into the RGB latent space via a feature merge block, and LoRA/DoRA adapters can be fully merged into the base Wan model, adding zero extra inference cost—this is a genuine advantage over TransPixeler's alpha-token/duplicated-backbone design.

The VAE design (random hard rendering over a color set, soft/hard render losses, Sobel edge loss) is a reasonable and clearly described adaptation of LayerDiffuse-style latent transparency to video, with sensible use of causal 3D convolutions for temporal merging.
Qualitative results are impressive in places (semi-transparent objects, glowing effects, hair strands), and the paper is honest about failure cases (Figure 19-20).
The paper appears to release model weights, which supports reproducibility of the inference pipeline.
weaknesses: The evaluation is entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative metrics whatsoever—no FVD or motion metrics for video quality, no alpha/transparency quality measures (e.g., SAD, MSE, gradient error against composited ground truth), no reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) for the VAE, and no user study. The central claims of 'superior performance in visual quality, motion realism, and transparency rendering' are supported only by cherry-picked figure comparisons.

The comparison protocol against TransPixeler is not fair or controlled. Wan-Alpha is prompted in Chinese with its own hand-tuned style tags ('Close-up', 'Realistic style', 'transparent background'), while baselines receive short English prompts, and prompt-extension is applied to the proposed model but not the baselines. Differences in prompt specificity and style tags alone could explain much of the visible quality gap; the paper does not control for this.

The text-to-video training set is extremely small (301 videos + 20 images + 116 web videos, i.e., 437 captioned samples, 1,500 iterations), and the captioning pipeline relies on manual refinement of every caption. This raises questions about generalization beyond the narrow distribution of matting datasets and web videos, and the claimed diversity is hard to verify from curated figures.

No ablation studies are provided. The contributions of the feature merge block design, the color-set rendering strategy, individual loss terms, DoRA vs. LoRA, and dataset curation choices are all unverified.

There is no quantitative VAE comparison against LayerDiffuse or AlphaVAE, despite the paper positioning its VAE as a core contribution; claims that prior VAE approaches are 'less effective' for video are not substantiated experimentally.

Novelty is limited: the method is essentially a combination of existing components (LayerDiffuse-style latent transparency, frozen Wan-VAE, LoRA/DoRA fine-tuning, LightX2V distillation) applied to a new base model, with the dataset curation being the main empirical contribution.

Presentation issues: the abstract's release URL is blank; several claims (e.g., '15 times faster') conflate differences in base model, resolution, FPS, and frame count rather than isolating the method's efficiency; and the stated focus of prior work on 'visual quality' vs. the paper's own goals is asserted without evidence.

The paper states results were generated 'without any hardware-specific acceleration' but reports 128 seconds for 81 frames at 832x480 without specifying hardware or sampler settings used for the baseline, making the efficiency claim hard to verify.

strengths: Practical and efficient design: the RGBA VAE reuses the pretrained Wan-VAE (frozen encoders, LoRA-adapted decoders, a lightweight feature-merge block), and the DiT is adapted with a single DoRA. This adds zero extra inference cost and avoids TransPixeler's alpha-token/duplicated-backbone overhead, which is a meaningful engineering contribution.

Impressive qualitative results: Figures 1, 10-18 show convincing transparency rendering including semi-transparent objects, glowing effects, fluids, and fine hair detail, which are known failure modes of prior work (e.g., Alfie cannot generate semi-transparent objects).

The rendering-based VAE training objectives (soft/hard rendering with random background colors, composite L1 + perceptual + Sobel edge losses) are a reasonable and clearly motivated design for injecting alpha into an RGB latent space without KL divergence issues.

The curated data strategy (careful selection from matting datasets plus manually verified captions with attribute tags) is well documented, and the paper is candid about dataset construction (sources, splits: 77,237 training / 4,066 validation videos for the VAE).
Supports practical deployment: 4-step, CFG-free sampling via LightX2V, weights mergeable into the base model, and stated intent to release the model, which increases usefulness and reproducibility.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges failure cases (unintended background debris, alpha masks with holes/missing regions).
weaknesses: Evaluation is entirely qualitative. Claims of 'superior performance in visual quality, motion realism, and transparency rendering' are supported only by cherry-picked side-by-side figures. There are no quantitative metrics (e.g., FVD, alpha SAD/gradient error, CLIP score), no user study, and no evaluation on a held-out prompt benchmark. For a paper whose central claim is quality, this is the most material weakness.

The comparison to TransPixeler is confounded: Wan-Alpha builds on Wan while TransPixeler builds on CogVideoX-5B, resolutions/FPS/frame counts differ (480x832@16FPS, 81 frames vs 480x720@8FPS, 49 frames), and Wan-Alpha uses its own style-tag-augmented prompts while TransPixeler uses the original prompts. The '15 times faster' claim largely reflects the different base model and LightX2V distillation rather than the paper's methodological contributions; this attribution is not disentangled.

No ablation studies. Key design choices are asserted without evidence: DoRA vs. LoRA for the DiT ('we found to yield better semantic alignment'), the feature-merge block architecture, the contribution of each loss term, the hard/soft rendering scheme, and the random-color rendering strategy. The VAE also lacks quantitative reconstruction evaluation (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS/alpha metrics).

The text-to-video fine-tuning set is extremely small (~437 samples with manually refined Chinese-only captions). Generalization to diverse prompts, languages, and open-vocabulary concepts is not evaluated; the 'model can also generate from English prompts' claim is supported only by anecdotal figures.

Novelty is moderate: the approach is largely a combination of LayerDiffuse-style latent transparency, LoRA/DoRA adaptation, and data curation applied to a stronger base model. The improvements over prior work may stem substantially from the base model (Wan) and data quality rather than methodological innovation; no experiment isolates this.

Reproducibility gaps: the release link in the abstract is blank ('available on our website: .'), the web-collected portion of the dataset and its licensing/copyright status are not detailed, and the manually curated caption set (a core asset) is not described in enough depth to reconstruct.

Minor presentation issues: Figures 19-20 referenced in the Limitations section are described inconsistently (Figure 19's caption describes a feature, not a failure), the abstract's claim of 'state-of-the-art' rests on a two-system visual comparison, and several technical details (e.g., how temporal consistency of alpha is enforced beyond the causal convolution, training compute) are underspecified.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically valuable task (RGB-A video generation), with a clearly articulated core problem: entanglement between RGB and alpha distributions in existing approaches (LayerDiffuse VAE adaptation, TransPixeler).

The two main technical ideas are intuitive and well-motivated: (i) the transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss ties VAE latent learning to the downstream DiT via a frozen DiT, shifting the alpha distribution in terms of likelihood rather than raw latent distance; (ii) the transparency-guided mean sampler injects a Gaussian ellipse prior into the diffusion noise, which doubles as a user-controllable transparency mechanism at inference.

Comprehensive experimental support: quantitative comparison against TransPixeler (open and closed variants), LayerFlow, and an additional LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff baseline (Table 1); user study on transparency correctness and overall quality (Table 2); ablations covering both VAE components (Table 3, Fig. 7) and the mean-shift strength (Fig. 8).

Strong practical advantages: significant inference efficiency (81 frames at 480x832, 16 FPS in 128s vs. 32 min for TransPixeler, 15x faster), compatibility with acceleration tools (LightX2V, 4 steps, no CFG), and no architectural duplication of the backbone.

Useful extensions demonstrating generality of the framework: transparency placement/shape control (Fig. 9) and image-to-video animation of transparent assets (Fig. 10), plus a curated RGB-A video dataset with captions and attribute labels.
Promised open-source release of model and dataset improves reproducibility and community value.
weaknesses: The bidirectional diffusion loss is heuristic and potentially unstable: inverting the sign of the rectified-flow loss (L_bidiff = M * L_RF) creates an unbounded-from-below objective in semi-transparent/transparent regions, effectively asking the frozen DiT to maximize its loss there. The paper provides intuition (likelihood shifting) but no theoretical or empirical analysis of why this does not diverge or degrade the shared latent space; no training stability results are reported.

Notational/technical inconsistency: Eq. (2) defines the velocity target as vt = epsilon - Z, while Eq. (13) defines v~t = Zt - epsilon~, which differs in sign under the same rectified-flow parameterization. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the formulation as written.

Details needed for reproducibility are missing: the definitions/thresholds separating opaque (O), semi-transparent (S), and transparent (T) regions used in the mask M are not given; the same symbol mu is overloaded for both the mean function mu(Z) and the scalar shift strength in Eq. (19); the project website URL is blank.

Evaluation of transparency quality relies primarily on a user study; no quantitative transparency metric (e.g., alpha accuracy, matte quality on held-out data) is reported, and user-study protocol details (number of participants, conditions) are sparse. VBench metrics are computed on white-background renderings, which does not directly measure alpha fidelity.

The generation ablation (Fig. 7) is qualitative only; there is no quantitative ablation isolating the mean sampler's contribution, nor an ablation of DoRA vs. LoRA despite the claim that DoRA performs better. Also missing: ablations on the rendering-loss variants and the ellipse-mask design.

The comparison setting is not fully controlled: baselines are built on different backbones (AnimateDiff, and TransPixeler's own base), and the closed-source TransPixeler variant on Adobe Firefly has unclear resolution/settings, so the large margins in Table 1 partly reflect the stronger Wan2.1-14B base model rather than the proposed components alone.

The RGB-A generation training set is very small (429 samples, of which only 301 are videos), and DiT training uses only 1,750 iterations; generalization behavior (e.g., complex multi-object scenes, occlusions, large transparent regions) is not systematically characterized, and the train/inference mismatch of the mean sampler (G derived from ground-truth alpha in training but user-defined/centered at inference) is discussed only briefly.

Transparency correctness claims in the qualitative comparisons (e.g., glass transparency errors attributed to RGB-alpha confusion in TransPixeler) are anecdotal and supported by a few cherry-picked examples rather than a systematic failure-mode analysis.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem (RGB-A video generation) with a clearly motivated core idea: shifting the alpha distribution while preserving the RGB distribution in both latent and noise spaces, rather than relying on architectural duplication.

The transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss is a clever and simple mechanism: introducing a frozen DiT into VAE training and inverting the RF loss sign in transparent regions directly ties latent-space learning to the generator's perception, addressing the stated gap between statistical separation and generation capability.

The transparency-guided mean sampler provides a dual benefit — a training prior that helps the DiT distinguish transparency, and an inference-time controllability knob (mask position/size), demonstrated qualitatively in Figs. 7–9 with a graceful failure mode (color bias) analyzed for the shift strength µ.

Strong empirical results: best scores across all VBench/OpenS2V metrics (Table 1) and a clear user-study preference (Table 2), plus a compelling practical argument on efficiency — no backbone duplication, LoRA/DoRA mergeability, LightX2V acceleration, and a reported 15× speedup over TransPixeler.

Additional contributions increase usefulness: a curated RGB-A video dataset with captions/attribute labels, a comparison against the generation+matting pipeline (Fig. 6), and an image-to-video extension (Fig. 10).
Promised open-source release of model and dataset supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The generative-training data is very small (429 samples) and the DiT is trained for only 1,750 iterations; the paper does not analyze how much of the performance gain comes from the proposed distribution-shifting techniques versus careful data curation and the strong Wan2.1 base model.

The headline claim is about shifting RGB-A distributions, but the evidence is indirect: Table 3 ablates only VAE reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), which do not directly validate that the alpha distribution is shifted or that the latent space is more 'distinguishable' to the DiT; no latent-space statistics, likelihood measurements, or generation-metric ablation of TABD are provided (Fig. 7 is qualitative only).

Notation inconsistencies undermine clarity: Eq. (2) defines vt = ϵ − Z while Eq. (13) defines v˜t = Zt − ϵ˜ (opposite sign conventions without explanation); the mask M uses regions O, S, T whose alpha thresholds are never specified; Eq. (19) reuses the symbol µ for both the mean function and the shift strength.

Evaluation details are thin: the user study's participant count, stimulus set, and protocol are unreported; text alignment of exactly 4.00 from a GPT-4o-based scorer looks suspiciously clean; the website URL in the abstract is blank, and several implementation details are deferred to supplementary material.

A mean-shift strength of µ = 0.05 on a [0,1]-normalized mask is a very small prior; the paper should better justify why such a subtle noise-mean shift is sufficient, especially given the reported red color bias at µ = 0.5.

Baselines are limited: the strongest competitor (TransPixeler closed-source) is evaluated only via Adobe Firefly outputs, and baseline implementations (e.g., LayerDiffuse+AnimateDiff) may not have been tuned to their best; the very small dataset raises questions about generalization beyond the tested prompts.

Several design choices appear heuristic (Gaussian ellipse fit, hard-alpha binarization at 0.5, fixed ellipse parametrization) without sensitivity analysis or discussion of when the single-ellipse assumption breaks down (e.g., multiple or non-convex foreground objects).
